A veterinary medical terminology table explicitly segments hematochezia with -chezia meaning defecation; Dictionary.com independently defines the English term and traces it to Greek defecation and -ia.

entries.meaning: Used to form names of muscarinic receptor agonists and antagonists.
entries.reason: Drug-name stem reference attributes -clidine/-clidinium to WHO naming conventions and lists procyclidine; NLM independently identifies procyclidine as a muscarinic antagonist. Specialized pharmaceutical name stem.

entries.meaning: Combining form of Colombia and Colombian.

entries.meaning: Forming the name of an epic about the indicated topic.

Wiktionary assigns gelatino-bromide to gelatino-; independent photographic history describes gelatino-bromide emulsion plates made with gelatin. Historical photographic terminology.

entries.meaning: saw; having an action or appearance like that of a saw
entries.reason: A conchology monograph explicitly parses Prionodesmacea as Greek prion saw plus desma ligament and associates it with saw teeth; MW lists it under priono-. Historical bivalve classification.

entries.origin: Abstracted from aerobe and microbe, ultimately Greek bios life
entries.reason: Collins directly analyzes aerobe as aer- plus (micr)obe and defines it as an oxygen-requiring organism; Wiktionary independently describes the extracted -obe element. Restricted to this biological back-formation, not any arbitrary -obe word.

Dictionary.com analyzes ovaritis as ovar(ium) plus -itis and defines the word as ovary inflammation. MW independently includes this exact term under the ovary sense. The ovarian-and sense remains unverified.
Wiktionary records the Moravian form; an independent geography source identifies Moravo-Silesian Region with the historical regions of Moravia and Silesia.

Cambridge English Dictionary gives topoi as plural of English topos; a historical Greek grammar independently identifies -oi as the masculine nominative plural ending. This is an inherited inflection used with specific Greek loans, not a standalone word base.

The source assigns zonoplacental to the zone or zonal sense; an independent scientific dictionary traces the first element to Latin zona, girdle, and defines a zonary placenta. The first numbered sense remains unresolved.

An independent historical scientific dictionary explains scapiflorous as having flowers on a scape from Latin scapus and flos; a botanical atlas confirms its sense. This supports the specialized scapi- plus flor- boundary.

entries.meaning: Characteristic of, pertaining to, or possessing a filiform structure.
entries.reason: An independent zoology teaching source explicitly analyzes nematode as nemat- thread plus -odes resembling; this supports the exact short form and threadlike sense.

Merriam-Webster gives Hamito-Semitic under hamito-; Collins independently explicitly analyzes Hamito- as a combining form of Hamitic. The language-family designation is historical and associated with an obsolete classificatory framework.

entries.meaning: having a specified number of units of prosodic time
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster supplies decasemic under -semic; the independently edited Century Dictionary defines the exact term as ten units of metrical measurement in ancient prosody.

An independent dictionary traces pectinate to Latin pectin- (comb) and defines it as having comb-like projections. This preserves the historical stem as a lookup form and does not confuse it with the unrelated plant polysaccharide pectin.

entries.meaning: Of or pertaining to the Nile.
entries.reason: A linguistic reference explains that Nilo-Saharan was named for languages along the Nile and in the Sahara, while Collins independently records the exact English term. The family designation remains a linguistic hypothesis rather than a claim of settled relationships.

Merriam-Webster lists emboliform for embolus; Taber independently relates the adjective to embolus plus -form and defines it as wedge-shaped. This is a historical plug-shaped lookup rather than a claim about blood clots; an alternative segmentation is embol- plus -iform.
Merriam-Webster gives hypertony under -tony; an independent clinical glossary lists hypertony as an alternative to hypertonia. The historical medical example denotes an abnormal degree of tone.
The source defines Nippo- as a form for Japan; an independent international art history article uses Nippo-Brazilian for Japanese immigrants and their descendants in Brazil.

The source gives tantaliferous for tantali-, and a European geological report independently uses tantaliferous for tantalum-bearing pegmatites. The historical lookup boundary overlaps an alternative analysis tantal- plus -iferous.

entries.meaning: Used to form the names of Wojak characters, or, by extension, caricaturized personifications of a given trait/quality.
entries.reason: An independent university analysis explicitly describes -oomer as a recurring Wojak suffix and explains zoomer as Generation Z plus -oomer; this sense is confined to the internet character and caricature convention.
The source lists secretin under secret- for secretion; an independent etymological dictionary gives secrete plus -in and a medical review confirms its role in secretion.

entries.meaning: Alternative form of nonadeca- used before a vowel.
entries.reason: The source gives nonadecane as a nineteen-carbon example; NIST independently lists its formula C19H40, confirming the exact chemical name and nineteen-carbon scope.
The source lists lobiform under lobi-; an independent university zoological glossary defines it as lobe-shaped. This is a historical lookup grouping alongside the alternative lob- plus -iform.

An independent clinical pharmacology reference explicitly identifies -osin in selective alpha-1 blockers and gives prazosin as an example. This documents the clinical naming pattern, without claiming every official naming stem is exactly -osin.

entries.meaning: of plants having such or so many pistils
entries.reason: The source treats -gynian as a form associated with -gynia in Linnaean botanical names; an independent botanical glossary records digynian for flowers with two styles or carpels. This is restricted to historical botanical terminology.

entries.meaning: Normandy, the Normans, or the Norman language.
entries.reason: The Oxford Dictionary of Family Names uses Normanno-Picard in English for names of Norman and Picard dialect origin and explains Norman as the language of Normandy.

entries.meaning: Having or equipped with a certain feature or structure.
entries.reason: Oxford directly analyzes eukaryote as eu- plus karyo- plus -ote and defines an organism having a distinct nucleus. The entry supports the structural-feature sense in biological terminology.

Merriam-Webster gives cionocranial for ciono- meaning pillar; the independently edited Century Dictionary defines it as having a column-skull and traces its element to Greek pillar. This is a historical zoological term.

entries.meaning: Used to form plurals of some Hebrew loanwords ending in -a or -ah.
entries.reason: Dictionary.com explicitly lists Halachoth as the plural of Halacha; the original source identifies -oth as a plural ending of Hebrew loanwords. A historical Judaica catalogue independently gives the same singular and plural. This records the ending itself, not the inflected plural as a separate root.

An invertebrate zoology dictionary defines scopiform as brush-shaped and derives it from Latin scopa and forma; the original source explicitly lists scopi- for brush with that word. The i is a historical linking vowel and this alias does not claim a unique modern segmentation against -iform.

entries.meaning: A variant of octo-, used for substitutions of eight complex rather than simple units
entries.reason: An American Chemical Society paper names octakis(dimethylamino)porphyrazine, with eight complex dimethylamino groups. The source defines octakis- as the chemistry multiplier for eight complex units. This is the chemical sense only, not the unreviewed polyhedron sense.

entries.meaning: Alternative form of -a-palooza without the -a-, found sometimes following a word which already ends in a vowel.
entries.reason: Columbia Journalism Review describes -palooza as an event-forming ending; a local news report independently uses PizzaPalooza for a pizza festival, with the final a of pizza immediately followed by palooza. This matches the specified alternate form.

A King's College London study explicitly uses Turco-Greek for political relations between Turkey and Greece; the source lists Turco-Greek in the Turkish-and sense. The separate Turkic and Turkish senses are not established by this example.

entries.meaning: Used to form names of heparin derivatives including low molecular mass heparins.
entries.reason: The WHO stem book explicitly assigns -parin to heparin derivatives and lists enoxaparin; MedlinePlus independently identifies enoxaparin as a low-molecular-weight heparin. This is the pharmaceutical naming stem.

An independent university linguistic resource uses Osco-Umbrian as the established label referring to Oscan and Umbrian, while warning that it is now dated. The source identifies Osco- as Oscan, and the hyphen is preserved.

Cambridge independently recognises haemacytometer as an English form for a blood-cell-counting instrument, and the original dictionary provides hema-/haema- in that same formation; a historical scientific instrument catalogue confirms the exact spelling and blood meaning. This avoids the vowel overlap in haemangioma.

An independent microscopy paper uses osmiophilic in describing structures stained by osmium; the original source assigns osmio- to osmium and identifies osmiophilic as an example. This is the osmium-stain sense, not osm- for smell or osmosis.

A microbiology dictionary specifically defines heterokont as referring to a pair of dissimilar flagella on a cell; the source defines -kont as flagellum of a cell. This establishes the flagellum sense rather than relying only on the name of a whole organism.

entries.meaning: Used to form adjectives indicating a fear of a specific thing.
entries.reason: Webster's New International Dictionary independently records claustrophobiac specifically as an adjective and refers to claustrophobic; the original suffix entry assigns -phobiac to fear adjectives. This does not decide the other noun or alternate senses of -phobiac.

Dictionary.com explicitly derives mercurate from mercury plus -ate and defines it as a salt containing mercury in a complex anion; an independent PubChem record also uses mercurate in a mercury compound name. This is the mercury sense rather than an astrology-related form.

The original Merriam-Webster entry explicitly assigns phycitol to phyc- (algae); NIST independently lists phycitol as erythritol and the Geneva chemistry handbook states that this compound is found in algae. This verifies the exact phyc- form, not merely phyco-.

An 1867 Chemical News paper on palladium compounds repeatedly uses palladio-protochloride as a standalone compound name, with chemical composition and context. Wiktionary independently specifies palladio- as palladium. The example is historical chemical nomenclature.

entries.meaning: dedicated to or newly aware of something
entries.origin: reanalysed from redpilled and similar internet slang
entries.reason: NPR's transcript independently explains -pilled as a productive suffix for getting enthusiastic about something and gives the actual example soccerpilled; Wiktionary records the same dedication or heightened-awareness suffix. The example is playful internet slang, not a claim about swallowing medication.

entries.meaning: of or pertaining to the pope or the papacy
entries.reason: The Century Dictionary explicitly derives papaphobia from medieval Latin papa, pope, plus Greek -phobia and defines dread or hatred of the pope or papacy. This independently supports the given papa- papal sense; it is a rare historical word, not a medical diagnosis.

entries.origin: Servian, historical English variant of Serbian
entries.reason: A 1907 English-language Hellenic Herald article describes a dialect as a Servo-Bulgarian mixture and contrasts Servian with Bulgarian; UCL independently identifies Servo-Bulgarian as Serbian-Bulgarian in an archive title. This confirms the historic Serbian form and distinguishes it from mechanical servo-.
MW gives lepidomelane under -melane; an independent geology manual defines it as black mica and parses its name from lepis scale and melas black. Historical mineralogical terminology.

entries.origin: New Latin from Greek rhētinē resin
entries.reason: An independent horticultural cyclopedia directly explains the former conifer genus Retinispora from Greek retine resin plus spora seed; Kew confirms it is now a synonym of Chamaecyparis. The similar retin- retina sense is separate.
MW lists pallidiflorous for pallidi- pale; an independent medical lexicon directly analyzes it from Latin pallidus pale and flos flower, defining it as pale-flowered.

entries.origin: Latin plus more plus quam than
entries.reason: Wiktionary records plusquam- and notes plusquamperfect; an independent historical Scots dictionary documents the exact English-form term meaning pluperfect and derives it from Latin plus quam perfectum. Historical grammatical terminology.

entries.meaning: one having a specified part in generic names
entries.origin: New Latin from Greek meris part
entries.reason: MW explicitly gives Piptomeris under -meris; an Australian botanical glossary explains its fall plus part name and Kew confirms this historic genus is now a synonym of Jacksonia.
Etymonline directly parses wastrel from waste plus the pejorative -rel; Oxford independently gives its meaning and waste plus -rel derivation. This decision concerns the pejorative sense only.

MW explicitly lists Mongolo-Tatar; an independent historical thesis identifies the Mongolo-Tatar designation in Russian historiography, explaining its historical ethnic context. The term is a historical label and not a claim of an established language family.

entries.meaning: various polymers of deoxynucleotides and their derivatives
entries.reason: Wiktionary lists polydeoxynucleotide for polydeoxy-; an independent biochemistry textbook defines a polydeoxynucleotide as a long chain of deoxynucleotide units. Specialized polymer naming.

entries.meaning: Used to form names of daunorubicin derivatives used as antineoplastics.
entries.reason: WHO assigns the -rubicin stem to antineoplastic daunorubicin derivatives and lists doxorubicin; an independent medical review identifies the rubicin class and discusses doxorubicin in cancer treatment.

entries.origin: New Latin from Greek oura tail
entries.reason: MW lists anourous for the alternative -ourous spelling; Collins independently defines anurous as tailless and traces it to an- plus Greek oura tail, supporting the alternate -urous spelling. Zoological terminology.

entries.meaning: Used to form various polymers of deoxyribonucleotides and their derivatives.
entries.reason: Wiktionary lists polydeoxyriboadenylate for the combining form; a biochemical paper independently uses the exact word as a DNA polymer primer. Specialized nucleic-acid terminology.

The original ichthyological publication directly derives Poecilurichthys from Greek variegated, tail and fish; initial poecil is followed by the tail component. MW independently records poecil- in the variegated sense. Historical scientific name.

entries.meaning: Having a specified number or type of meanings.
entries.reason: Wiktionary defines -semous as meaning-bearing; a Stanford linguistic textbook independently analyzes polysemous as Greek poly many plus sema sign and uses it for words having multiple senses.

American Heritage independently identifies thion- as sulfur and gives thionic; Collins defines thionic as pertaining to sulfur and traces it to Greek theion plus -ic. Other thion- chemistry senses in separate source entries are not conflated.

entries.meaning: Forming the names of polyribonucleotides and derived words
entries.reason: Wiktionary explicitly lists polyriboadenylate; an independent biochemical paper uses the exact term for the polymerization product poly(A) formed from ATP. Specialized nucleic-acid nomenclature.

entries.origin: Latin sequi follow, extracted from compounds
entries.reason: Wiktionary explicitly lists obsequy for the extracted historical -sequy; Etymonline independently traces the word through Latin obsequium and obsequi follow, with semantic influence from exsequiae. This is a historical stem, not a claim that modern obsequy means follow.

entries.meaning: formative or formed material as of a cell or tissue
entries.reason: MW explicitly lists karyoplasma under -plasma; an independent biological review describes karyoplasma as material of the cell nucleus and derives karyo from Greek nucleus. Specialized cytology.
The original source supplies Europeo-Asiatic for European and; an independently authored historical natural history journal uses the exact term for a biogeographic region.

entries.meaning: A diminutive suffix used to add an element of childishness, informality, affectionateness, or levity to a word.
entries.reason: A linguistic study identifies upsies as an example of playful child-oriented suffixation; the source supplies the up plus -sies analysis. It remains restricted to informal diminutive usage.
Merriam-Webster explicitly gives brachyphalangia under -phalangia; an independent medical article defines it as shortened phalanges, confirming this specialist medical relation.
The source names potassio-chromic sulphate; an independent historical English chemical text uses the exact multiword term with a potassium-containing formula.

The source gives granuliform under granuli-; an independent historical English dictionary derives granuliform from granulum and forma, while a specialist word-element reference explicitly gives granuli- plus -form. The form is a historical lookup grouping alongside granul- plus -iform.

entries.meaning: containing sodium in place of hydrogen, used in names of organic compounds
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster gives sodiomalonic ester for sodium replacing hydrogen; an independent organic chemistry text describes sodium ethoxide converting malonic ester into its sodium salt, sodiomalonic ester.
The source identifies racio- as race; a study independently uses racioethnic and explains that it combines race and ethnicity.

entries.meaning: infix denoting complete hydrogenation in names of cyclic bases
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster identifies the internal -pe- element in lupetidine as complete hydrogenation; a patent independently describes hydrogenation of 3,5-lutidine to 3,5-lupetidine. This is an infix, not an initial prefix or final suffix.

entries.meaning: creature with a specified kind of sawlike part in generic names
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster gives the sawfly genus Diprion under -prion; an independent zoological nomenclator explicitly explains its Greek components as twice and saw, and a Canadian government source confirms the genus.

entries.meaning: Used to form adjectives conveying an attitude of contempt or doubt over the subject's intelligence. (offensive)
entries.reason: Wiktionary directly gives libtarded as lib plus -tarded with the specified contemptuous sense; an independent first-person published account attests its use as an insult. The entry is confined to offensive derogatory language.

Merriam-Webster lists mimotype under mimo-; an independent zoological nomenclature compendium defines it as an analogous form resembling another in a different area. The relationship is resemblance and does not by itself assert biological defensive mimicry.

WHO identifies historical -terenol as an unofficial alternative to the -terol bronchodilator stem and lists soterenol; an independent pharmacology paper describes soterenol as a beta-adrenergic bronchodilator.

entries.meaning: Alternative form of Russo-. (rare historical spelling)
entries.reason: A naval museum catalog refers to the Russio- Japanese War, with a space after the hyphen; an independent English discussion spells the same historical war Russio-Japanese. This is a rare historical spelling of Russo-Japanese.

Merriam-Webster provides tesseradecade under tessera- meaning four; an independent scholarly thesis uses tesseradecades for sets of fourteen generations. The term is historical, especially in biblical commentary.
Wiktionary gives sado- as sadism and Collins independently defines sadomasochism as sadism and masochism combined.
A Cambridge geography chapter uses Saharo-Sahelian for the transition at the Sahara–Sahel boundary, independently supporting the source’s Sahara sense.

An independent historical English dictionary records coronofacial and explains its angle using the coronal suture and facial line. The source assigns corono- specifically the combined coronal-and sense; this rare anatomical form is distinct from the similarly spelled coronary and crown senses.

entries.meaning: ones related to or characterized by, in biological taxonomic names
entries.origin: New Latin, from Latin neuter plural -ina
entries.reason: Collins records acarine and explicitly derives the New Latin taxonomic name Acarina from Acarus plus -ina, identifying the group of mites and ticks. Webster's taxon headword independently records the same formation. This biological suffix has a different sense from the existing -ina for musical instruments; Acarina is a historical taxonomic name whose rank and modern classification vary.

A United Nations conservation report explicitly describes Sahelo-Saharan habitats as comprising the Sahel and Sahara ecoregions; the African Union independently uses the same adjective for the Sahelo-Saharan zone. The word is a geographic relational form.

The English Japanese Pharmacopoeia records salazosulfapyridine as a drug name and gives its chemical structure; an independent English product monograph identifies it as phenylazosalicylic acid derivative sulfasalazine. This confirms the exact initial salazo- in pharmaceutical naming.

PubChem independently lists nicotinonitrile and nicotinic acid nitrile as synonyms for the same chemical compound, and the source dictionary explicitly gives the example for nicotino- with the nicotinic acid meaning. The nicotine/tobacco sense remains unresolved in this decision.

entries.meaning: one having a specified nose, in zoological genus names
entries.origin: New Latin, from Greek rhis, rhinos, nose
entries.reason: A zoological nomenclature article coins Notiorhinus, explicitly derives rhinus from Greek for nose and says the name refers to the animal's pointed head; the original reference defines -rhinus in zoological genus names. This valid replacement name avoids the preoccupied Megarhinus example.

entries.meaning: anion formally derived by adding a hydride ion to a parent hydride
entries.reason: IUPAC's nomenclature recommendations explicitly specify -uide for addition of a hydride ion to a parent hydride, and give boranuide from borane as the example. This precisely verifies the specialized anion sense and boundary.

entries.meaning: ones having a specified seed or germ, in higher botanical taxon names
entries.reason: A Smithsonian systematic treatment independently documents Rhodospermeae as Harvey's 1853 historical grouping of red algae, exactly the taxonomic example given by the source for -spermeae. It is a historical botanical group name, not a claim that red algae literally have seeds.

The linguistics programme Because Language discusses the attested construction money schmoney and explicitly characterizes it as dismissive schm-reduplication. The example is an entire fixed reduplicated expression: schm- attaches at the start of the second word schmoney, not at the beginning of the full phrase.

A historical Dictionary of Scientific Terms independently records hemiplegy as paralysis of one side of the body and gives its Greek roots; the source dictionary supplies the exact -plegy combining form for a specified paralysis. This is an old variant of hemiplegia.

entries.meaning: something likened to female genitalia (vulgar slang)
entries.reason: Dictionary.com independently defines bussy as vulgar slang for the male anus and explicitly derives it as boy + pussy. The American Dialect Society describes -ussy as a reanalyzed productive suffix and cites bussy; this supports the specified sexually analogous sense only, with its slang register.

entries.meaning: selenium replacing an atom in the named molecule
entries.reason: IUPAC gives selenacyclopentane for a five-membered ring with selenium in place of a carbon; a Michigan State organic chemistry resource independently lists selena as the skeletal replacement prefix for selenium. This confirms the chemical replacement sense in an initial position.

An independent internet-slang account identifies huzz as the plural form underlying the -uzz series and relates it to hoes; Wiktionary explicitly parses hoe + -uzz. The word is derogatory slang, and other -uzz formations may also be singular or collective.

The Century Dictionary independently records sacciform as sack-shaped from Latin saccus and forma, while Webster explicitly assigns that exact word to sacci-. The competing sacc- plus -iform analysis is possible, so the edge is the source dictionary's explicit morphological analysis, not an assertion that other segmentations are impossible.

entries.meaning: tilted position of an anatomical structure
entries.reason: A medical terminology textbook analyzes anteversion as ante- plus -version and explains it as forward tipping of the uterus; an independent historic English medical work gives the same composition and sense. This establishes the anatomical position sense, distinct from other senses of version.

entries.origin: New Latin Laurus via lauric acid
entries.reason: The CDC's historical Registry of Toxic Effects independently lists lauromitrile as a chemical name, while the source dictionary explicitly gives that spelling under lauro- meaning lauric acid. The alternative laurel sense remains unresolved. The registry is indexed under an old synonym and may preserve historical nomenclature.

entries.meaning: Having a certain number of broods or generations in a year.
entries.origin: French -voltin from Italian volta time and -in
entries.reason: An independent invertebrate zoology dictionary defines univoltine as one generation yearly and derives it from Latin unus one and Italian volta time. Wiktionary defines the -voltine element for brood or generation count.

entries.meaning: sponges in names of orders and other higher groups of sponges
entries.reason: MW directly lists Silicispongiae under -spongiae; an independent molecular phylogeny paper explains that historical Silicispongiae grouped the siliceous sponges. Historical zoological group.

entries.origin: New Latin from Greek rhipis fan
entries.reason: Chambers directly parses Rhipicera as Greek rhipis fan plus keras horn; CSIRO independently identifies the beetle genus and fanlike antennae. Zoological genus naming.

entries.meaning: Used to form names of antineoplastics and antivirals of the zidovudine type
entries.reason: WHO stem book identifies -vudine with zidovudine-type antivirals and antineoplastics and lists stavudine; MedlinePlus independently identifies stavudine as an HIV antiviral.

entries.meaning: Relating to Somalia, the Somali peninsula, or the Somali people, language, or culture.
entries.reason: Wiktionary supplies the Somali-related combining element; an independent regional news article uses Somalo-Ethiopian for relations between Somalia and Ethiopia.
Wiktionary analyzes hamwich as ham plus sandwich or -wich; an independent UK intellectual-property decision discusses HAMWICH as a ham and sandwich reference with suffix WICH. Informal blend.

MW explicitly lists Libyo-Phoenician as Libyan and Phoenician; an independent historical encyclopedia explains the label in terms of Libyan and Phoenician. A modern study disputes specific cultural applications, so the example is a historical label rather than proof of an ethnic classification.

Webster’s 1924 dictionary directly lists manganoso-manganic oxide under the manganous combining form; a separate chemistry handbook describes that exact historic mixed oxide and formula. The example is an attested multiword technical compound, not an isolated adjective.
MW cites salinometer for the saline sense; Collins independently defines it as a salt-measuring device and analyzes saline plus -o- plus -meter. A separate saline-and sense remains unverified.

Wiktionary identifies -xor as a leet respelling; the University of Michigan thesis independently attests haxxor as a leet rendering of hacker. The overlapping -xxor spelling is a variant, so this is restricted to informal spelling practice.

entries.meaning: higher taxon with a specified type of eyes
entries.reason: MW explicitly parses -ophthalma and cites Edriophthalma; Darwin Correspondence independently discusses this historical arthropod taxon and its sessile eyes. The example is historical taxonomic usage.
MW directly associates ichn- with ichnology; an independent fossil reference analyzes ichn as trace or track and -ology as study, while describing the science of trace fossils.

Wiktionary identifies sulphureo-saline under this combining form; an independent historical medical cyclopaedia uses the exact adjective for a state involving sulphur and saline properties. This is historical terminology.

Merriam-Webster supplies purpuriparous for purpuri-; an independently edited historical dictionary defines it as producing a purple secretion and traces the compound to purpura and parere. This is a specialist biological word.

entries.meaning: Used as a substitute for -s in marking the plural of nouns. Usually used in words in which the -s suffix is actually pronounced /z/. (nonstandard spelling)
entries.reason: A linguistic dissertation independently documents dogz as a stylized spelling of plural dogs and explicitly discusses z replacing plural s. This is an informal spelling variant, not a separate pronunciation or a claim that all plurals normally use z.

Merriam-Webster cites menthone under menth- for menthol; an independent historical reference reports production of menthone by oxidizing menthol. This is a chemical naming relation, not an assertion that the substances are identical.

Etymonline independently analyzes symmetrophobia as a symmetry combining form plus -phobia; Collins confirms the exact term and its meaning. It also has a historical architectural sense of avoidance, as noted in the source.

Collins directly analyzes phosphine as phosph- plus -ine and identifies it as phosphorus hydride, confirming source sense 2. A separate historical pharmaceutical reference identifies phosphergot as a mixture of sodium phosphate and ergot, supporting source sense 1. Further independent search found phosphocreatine described as creatine with phosphoric acid, but its boundary is phospho-, not the requested phosph-, so phosphoric acid remains unresolved.

The historical ethnonym Tataro-Mongolian describes the Mongol peoples also referred to as Tatars in an English-language history of Kyrgyzstan. This supports the Tatar ethnonym in a historical compound; it does not independently establish the Tatarstan geographic sense.

The Century Dictionary independently analyzes sphenotresia from Greek wedge plus perforation; a veterinary history describes the operation as perforation of the skull. The word is historical specialist terminology.

entries.meaning: Forms nicknames, especially of personal names (originally Australian English).
entries.reason: An Australian university guide independently describes the suffix -zza in Australian nicknames and gives Gary becoming Gazza. This is the nickname-forming sense, historically associated with Australian English.

A neuroscience paper describes the tectopontine tract as originating in the midbrain tectum and descending toward the pons; a second neuroanatomy resource describes the same connection. This confirms the anatomical tectum sense.

Merriam-Webster cites ludicropathetic and specifies the combining form as ludicrous and; Mrs. Byrne’s independent unusual-word dictionary defines the whole exact word as ludicrous and pathetic. This is an obscure literary formation.

An independent historical medical dictionary gives anomalocephalus and directly derives it from Greek anomalos, irregular, and kephalē, head. It defines the obsolete medical term as a person whose head is deformed.

entries.meaning: having such or so many leaves (botanical)
entries.reason: A separately edited historical dictionary defines centifolious as having a hundred leaves and derives it from Latin centum and folium. Merriam-Webster independently specifies -folious for leaves and supplies that same exact word; the example is botanical.

A historical English dictionary explicitly defines Teuto- as Teuton or Teutonic and cites Teuto-Celtic; an independent historical journal uses the term for a combination of Teutonic and Celtic peoples. The example is historical terminology, not the separate Germany/German sense.

entries.meaning: Patronymic surname ending, an alternative form of -son (chiefly names of Scandinavian origin).
entries.reason: A Brigham Young University genealogy reference explains -sson as a Scandinavian patronymic ending and lists Jansson among surnames documented in the American record. It is a surname element of Scandinavian origin, not a claim of productive modern common-noun derivation.

entries.origin: New Latin from Greek nykteris, bat
entries.reason: The authors of the zoological description of Pilonycteris explicitly derive its name from pilo, hairy, plus Greek nycteris, bat. This is a scientific generic-name element and the example is a taxonomic name, not a common English word.

An independent historical botanical article uses the exact English description spinoso-dentate for leaves and notes the spines, consistent with the source analysis spinose and; a botanical Latin dictionary translates the corresponding form as spine-toothed.

entries.origin: Greek ōpos, genitive of ōps, eye
entries.reason: Etymonline independently traces myope through French and Latin to Greek myōps, literally closing the eyes, and gives the Greek eye element ōps, genitive ōpos. The example is an inherited medical borrowing rather than a modern productive formation.

entries.origin: Latin saccus, bag, and Greek sakkos
entries.reason: The Century Dictionary directly analyzes the English adjective saccobranchiate as Greek sack plus gills and defines it as having saccate gills. This exact English word establishes sacco- independently of the questionable historical genus Saccomys.

A number-naming table specifically describes the Conway–Wechsler system and lists tredecillion as the thirteenth -illion, with tre- representing three before decillion; a separate numerical reference traces the underlying Conway–Guy naming system. The use is confined to large-number nomenclature.

The WHO INN stem book directly gives -dan for pimobendan-type cardiac stimulants and lists adibendan; independently, PubChem's DrugBank record identifies the exact -dan in adibendan and the same class. This is specialized generic drug naming.

An independent English Flora of Siberia botanical treatment uses serratodentate for leaf edges; the source dictionary explicitly assigns it to serrato- meaning serrate and. This is specialized botanical terminology.

An English news report uses Turkmeno-Afghan for a border crossing from Turkmenistan to Afghanistan; an academic study independently discusses Turkmenistan's Afghan border. The verified example is the geographic Turkmenistan-related sense.

A Cambridge University Press African history article explicitly relates Ugando-Rwandan conflict to the forces of Uganda and Rwanda, while the source records Ugando- from Uganda. This independently confirms the geographic relational meaning.

entries.meaning: of or relating to the umbilicus
entries.reason: An English anatomical paper entitled Observations on the Umbilico-Mesenteric Vessels describes vessels running to the umbilicus. The source defines umbilico- as pertaining to the umbilicus; the compound is the single hyphenated adjective umbilico-mesenteric.

Wiktionary independently documents oniric as an English adjective meaning dreamlike and quotes its medical use; the source identifies onir- as a variant of the Greek-derived dream form. The spelling is distinct from oneiric and is rare.

entries.meaning: person with a tendency or strong attraction toward something
entries.reason: Dictionary.com lists bibliophiliac specifically as the noun related to bibliophilia, defined there as enthusiasm for books. The source assigns the -philiac ending a person-denoting use; the separately listed adjective sense is not assumed.

An architecture dictionary records amphistylar as having columns on both sides or ends; Collins independently gives the same sense and Greek pillar etymology. The source explicitly lists this example for -stylar and its architectural sense.

A linguistic historical paper discusses Uralo-Altaic as a proposed grouping of Uralic and Altaic languages; a modern scholarly paper notes that this proposed macrofamily is not established. This is evidence for the historical term, not an endorsement of the language-family hypothesis.

An independent English dermatology handbook describes liodermia as glossy skin that appears smooth; the Merriam-Webster entry identifies lio- as the smooth form. This historical medical term confirms the shorter spelling without an e.

entries.meaning: forms long-scale number names equal to 10^(6n+3)
entries.reason: South African official measurement rules identify trilliard as 10^21; the source describes -illiard as the long-scale 10^(6n+3) number suffix and trilliard as tri- plus -illiard. This is a long-scale usage, not the short-scale trillion.

A scientific affix dictionary explicitly gives konio- as dust and koniometer as an example; NIOSH independently documents the koniometer as a historical workplace aerosol particle measurement instrument. This is specialist dust-measurement terminology.

The advocacy pledge identifies -misic as an ending for hatred; Planned Parenthood independently uses transmisic and explains the related transmisia. A newly searched trans-language glossary also documents transmisic. The term is contemporary advocacy usage; it does not rely on UCLA's reproduction of Planned Parenthood content.

entries.meaning: nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist or partial agonist
entries.origin: pharmaceutical nomenclature stem, possibly nicotine and choline
entries.reason: WHO's nomenclature stem book directly lists -nicline for nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonists and varenicline among its examples; PubChem separately identifies varenicline as a nicotinic receptor partial agonist. This is an international drug-naming stem.

entries.meaning: spironolactone-derived aldosterone antagonist in drug names
entries.reason: WHO's 2013 stem book identifies -renone in spironolactone-derived aldosterone antagonists and explicitly lists mespirenone; PubChem independently describes mespirenone as a spironolactone derivative and aldosterone antagonist. WHO subsequently widened the stem definition to mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
An English word-parts dictionary explicitly assigns iono- to ionosphere; Etymonline independently explains ionosphere as an atmospheric region named for its ions and derived from ion and -sphere.

Wiktionary analyzes tubulitis as tubule plus -itis, with loss of the final e before the vowel; the independent NIEHS renal pathology resource defines it as inflammatory cells invading renal tubule epithelium. This supports the tubule sense; the separate microtubule sense remains untested.

entries.origin: Latin Batavi, an ancient people of the Netherlands
entries.reason: The Canadian government's English-language writing guide defines Batavo- as Dutch or Netherlands; the Batavophone English headword identifies Batavo- plus -phone, defines the word as Dutch-speaking, and cites two English published uses. This is the Dutch sense, not the separately listed Batavia sense.
Dictionary.com analyzes Slavophile as Slavo- plus -phile and defines it in relation to the Slavs; the independent American Heritage entry confirms the English headword and its cultural sense.

entries.origin: Latin aelurus, from Greek ailouros, cat
entries.reason: The University of Salamanca medical etymological dictionary analyzes elurophobia as cat plus fear and gives the English spelling; the US National Library of Medicine independently records elurophobia as fear of cats. The variant spelling is supported in specialized terminology.

A biogeographic glossary explicitly defines English boreo-alpine as a northern and mountain distribution; a peer-reviewed zoological paper independently uses the exact closed form boreoalpine for a species occurring in subarctic and alpine areas. This supports the northern element in specialist ecology.

entries.meaning: class III antiarrhythmic in sematilide-related drug names
entries.reason: The WHO stem book explicitly assigns -ilide to class III antiarrhythmics in the sematilide family and lists ibutilide. DailyMed independently describes ibutilide as a class III antiarrhythmic. Identical endings in unrelated drug names are not evidence of this sense.
Wiktionary identifies lepro- with leprosy; an independently published dictionary gives the scientific term leprology as lepra plus connecting -o- and -logy and defines it as study of leprosy.
WHO directly identifies -tizide as a naming stem and lists altizide; PubChem independently confirms altizide as a thiazide diuretic. This is a nomenclature class.
WHO explicitly lists eniporide under the Na+/H+ antiport inhibitor stem -poride; PubChem independently identifies the drug and its stem.
Taber’s medical dictionary independently identifies aque- as water and analyzes aqueduct as aque- plus duct; the original Wiktionary sense relates it to aqua-.
Wiktionary explicitly analyzes lienorenal as lieno- plus renal; an independent surgical anatomy text describes the lienorenal ligament as connecting the spleen and kidney.
WHO classifies -onidine as the clonidine-related antihypertensive stem and lists moxonidine; PubChem independently identifies moxonidine as an antihypertensive.
WHO classifies -serpine for Rauwolfia alkaloids and lists reserpine; an independent drug database identifies the alkaloid and its plant source.

IUPAC explicitly gives chloroformyl- and chloroformylacetic acid with a -COCl group; an independent chemistry paper uses the exact chemical name. Acyl chloride is the broader class, not an exact synonym for this substituent.
WHO identifies -dralazine as the hydrazinephthalazine antihypertensive stem and lists cadralazine; an independent drug reference lists the same drug in this class.
Wiktionary identifies Scotto- as a variant of Scoto-; an independent university review uses Scotto-Irish explicitly for cultural connections between Scotland and Ireland.
WHO identifies -pamil as the calcium-channel blocker stem and explicitly gives verapamil; Wiktionary independently lists the suffix and drug.
WHO classifies -prilat as diacid ACE inhibitor analogues and lists enalaprilat; independent clinical research identifies enalaprilat as the active diacid metabolite of enalapril.
Wiktionary identifies Balkano- as Balkan plus -o-; an independent linguistic study uses balkano-romanization for a historical Balkan-language process.
WHO’s INN stem reference lists -kiren for renin inhibitors including aliskiren; MedlinePlus independently identifies aliskiren as a direct renin inhibitor.

entries.meaning: South Slavic; Yugoslav in historical usage
entries.reason: Wiktionary identifies Jugo- as a Yugo- variant; the Library of Congress independently records the English historical Jugo-Slav movement associated with South Slavic and Yugoslav identity.
WHO lists carboprost under its prostaglandin naming stem prost; PubChem independently identifies carboprost as a prostaglandin analogue.
Wiktionary identifies Yugo- as Yugoslav; a US State Department historical document uses Yugo-American for groups in America connected with Yugoslavia.
WHO identifies -metacin as an indometacin-derived anti-inflammatory stem and lists acemetacin; PubChem independently describes acemetacin as an indometacin ester and anti-inflammatory agent.

entries.meaning: anti-inflammatory agents in the ibufenac group
entries.reason: WHO lists aceclofenac under -clofenac in its anti-inflammatory ibufenac group; PubChem independently describes the compound.
The source defines Hungaro- as Hungarian; the Croatian Supreme Court independently uses Hungaro-Croatian for a Hungary–Croatia agreement.

entries.meaning: anti-inflammatory agents in the ibufenac group
entries.reason: WHO explicitly lists lonazolac under the -zolac anti-inflammatory stem; PubChem independently describes lonazolac as a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory.
The anatomical terminology project analyzes pubo as the pubis morpheme in pubococcygeus; an independent anatomy review attests the muscle name and its pubic relation.
An English-language historical study explicitly discusses a Bulgaro-Greek conflict between Bulgarians and Greeks, confirming the Bulgaria/Bulgarian element in that historical compound.
A University of Southampton historical thesis uses Polonophile for a friend of Poland, independently confirming the Poland element followed by -phile.

entries.meaning: forms names of quinoline derivatives, especially antimalarial drugs
entries.reason: The World Health Organization explicitly identifies quine as a drug-name element for antimalarials containing a quinoline group and lists chloroquine in its stem compendium. This confirms the quinoline derivative sense in the antimalarial naming subset.

entries.meaning: drug-name stem for phenylazosalicylic acid derivatives
entries.reason: WHO groups -salazine among names for phenylazosalicylic-acid derivatives and explicitly lists sulfasalazine; the FDA label independently identifies that exact drug as a phenylazo salicylic acid.
A historical archaeology conference uses Britanno-Roman for Roman-period Britain; the formation is historical and relates to Britannia, not modern British nationality generally.
The historical study describes the Siamo-Burmese Gospel Team as a joint Thai-Burmese team, directly establishing the Siam component in this English historical compound.
WHO explicitly lists rasburicase among uricases named with -icase; the FDA independently identifies rasburicase as recombinant urate oxidase.
Dictionary.com explicitly analyzes Balto-Slavic as Balto- plus Slavic; Cambridge independently defines it as involving Baltic and Slavic languages.
WHO directly identifies the -semide stem as diuretics of the furosemide type and lists torasemide; a pharmacological review independently identifies torasemide as a loop diuretic.
The English dictionary analyzes Celto-Germanic as Celto- plus Germanic; the University of Wales study applies it to vocabulary of the Celtic and Germanic languages.
WHO explicitly assigns milrinone to the -rinone amrinone-derived cardiac stimulant stem; NLM identifies milrinone as an amrinone derivative and cardiotonic.

entries.meaning: Hurrian or the Hurrians (ancient history and linguistics)
entries.reason: The specialist Cuneiform Digital Library Journal explicitly uses Hurro-Urartian for the Hurrian and Urartian language family, matching the source formation and ancient-language scope.

entries.meaning: dopamine-related names used in antiparkinsonian drugs (drug nomenclature)
entries.reason: WHO classifies levodopa under the -dopa dopamine-related stem used in antiparkinsonism, and the German neurology guideline independently identifies levodopa as a Parkinson treatment; levodopa is a dopamine precursor rather than an ordinary direct receptor agonist.
A University of Munich historical paper uses Prusso-Austrian for the 1866 competition between Prussia and Austria, establishing the historical geographic element.
WHO assigns pergolide to -golide dopamine receptor agonists of the ergoline class; the independently issued manufacturer information names pergolide and its ergoline chemical structure.
Canada’s language portal defines the combining form Scando- and explicitly gives Scandoromani; a linguistic study independently describes the Swedish and Norwegian language variety.

entries.meaning: ACAT inhibitors investigated as antihyperlipidemics (drug nomenclature)
entries.reason: WHO names the -imibe inhibitor class and lists avasimibe; a clinical trial independently identifies avasimibe as an ACAT inhibitor investigated for combined hyperlipidemia. The compound was investigational, not asserted to be an approved treatment.

An English linguistics publication calls medieval Zadar Romance Dalmato-Romance; an Oxford study uses the same term for Dalmatian Romance varieties, establishing the geographic and linguistic element.

WHO lists -dilol under vasodilators and includes carvedilol; independent labeling identifies carvedilol as an adrenergic blocker. The beta-blocker property is specific to the example and is not asserted for every -dilol drug.

An American Journal of Archaeology review uses Illyro-Roman for society in the Roman-era Illyrian region; the source relates Illyro- to Illyria. A historical monograph independently uses Illyro-Roman in the same geographic context.

The Universal Decimal Classification uses Umbro-Sabellian as a language-family label that includes Umbrian; a history of Roman Italy independently relates the Umbro-Sabellian peoples to the Umbrian language. This is historical linguistic terminology.

WHO's drug-stem book lists acenocoumarol under -arol for dicoumarol-family anticoagulants; PubChem independently identifies acenocoumarol as an anticoagulant coumarin derivative. This is nomenclature classification, not a claim that all -arol endings have this meaning.

A published linguistic conference paper writes (Bosno-)Serbo-Croatian and explicitly explains the Bosno- part as Bosnian; an international court transcript independently uses Bosno-Croato-Serbian in discussion of Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian. The example is a linguistic label, not a statement about language status.

entries.origin: atropisomer, ultimately Greek atropos, not turning
entries.reason: The source explicitly lists atroposelective under atropo-, an alternative to the atropisomer element. A chemistry journal uses atroposelective for selection among structures whose chirality stems from hindered rotation, independently establishing the English specialist usage.

entries.meaning: fibrinogen receptor antagonist in drug names
entries.origin: pharmaceutical stem from fibrinogen and antagonist
entries.reason: The WHO nomenclature book explicitly assigns -fiban to fibrinogen receptor antagonists and lists tirofiban; an independent pharmacology research article calls tirofiban a specific fibrinogen receptor antagonist.

A hermeneutics textbook explicitly explains grammatico-historical as interpretation governed by grammar and history, and an independent university thesis describes the method using grammatical analysis and historical context. This is a historical theological term.

entries.origin: Latin oliva, olive, applied to olive-shaped brain structure
entries.reason: A neuroscience textbook explains that the olivocerebellar tract carries axons from the inferior olive to the cerebellum; an independent university neuroanatomy teaching sheet shows the same pathway. This supports the brain structure sense rather than olive fruit.
WHO explicitly groups rimantadine under -mantadine for adamantane derivatives; a separate medicinal chemistry paper identifies rimantadine among biologically active aminoadamantanes.
